newsitem.title: INDIA: Kashmir poll unlikely to end separatist campaign.
newsitem.headline: Kashmir poll unlikely to end separatist campaign.

text.p: India's move to restore a democratic government in the troubled Kashmir region through a tightly guarded state election is unlikely to end a six-year old revolt soon, political analysts said on Tuesday.

They said a new government in the state of Jammu and Kashmir would have to pursue a tough line against separatist militants with the help of the army and paramilitary forces, failing which the Himalayan region could slide into further chaos.

Dozens of separatist groups fighting Indian rule in Kashmir have opposed the four-stage elections, the first in the region for nine years, which are aimed at ending more than six years of direct rule by New Delhi.

At least 20 people, mostly political activists, have been killed during campaigning. Several candidates, including Farooq Abdullah, head of the state's largest party the National Conference, have escaped attacks.
The government says the first two phases of the elections on September 7 and 16 were fair and peaceful, a claim denied by separatists groups.
The next two rounds are on September 21 and 30. Results are expected in the first week of October.

"I fear this normalcy we have achieved could be diverted to create an even more dangerous situation," former junior interior minister Sibtey Razi told a news conference in Kashmir's summer capital of Srinagar.
"Post-election developments will be more important than this current phase of politics," he said.
Razi, campaigning in Kashmir for former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao's Congress party, accused the National Conference of being weak in its intentions of curbing separatist violence.
He said former National Conference chief minister Farooq Abdullah was being helped by "some official quarters" to win the state polls, suggesting the contest was not entirely fair.
Abdullah, widely tipped to win the elections, has often been accused by successive ruling parties in New Delhi, including the Congress party, of being soft on separatist militants.

The National Conference boycotted parliamentary elections in Kashmir in May, saying New Delhi was not seriously committed to granting greater autonomy to mainly Hindu India's only Moslem-majority state.
But Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda, whose United Front alliance is seen as sympathetic to the National Conference, has pledged "maximum autonomy" to the state following elections.
The proposal has not found much favour with the security forces who say any move to dilute their role in handling Kashmir could make their task difficult.
Indian security officials privately say while separatist violence had been curbed to some extent in the Kashmir valley, their hunt for the guerrillas was far from over.
"We have not said and cannot say in the near future that militancy has been removed from Kashmir," a senior official in charge of Kashmir's anti-guerrilla operations told Reuters.
"In fact, some level of pro-Pakistan feelings have always been there and will remain that way," he said, asking not be identified. "The elections are not going to change that equation very much."
More than 20,000 people have been killed since 1990 when simmering discontent against Indian rule turned into an armed revolt in Kashmir.
India accuses neighbouring Pakistan of training and arming separatist militants. Islamabad says it gives only political support to some of the groups.
